title: Why Listening Needs to Be Taught
brief: Open by establishing that listening is a skill requiring deliberate classroom attention, not simply exposure. Draw on the source's statement that audio materials help students develop and improve listening comprehension, hear new vocabulary in context, make connections between sounds and written words, and be exposed to different accents. Explain that teachers can integrate audio into lessons by creating activities where instructions and tasks are presented in audio format so students must use listening skills rather than reading skills, and note the fallback options the source provides when audio technology is unavailable (dictation tasks or guest speakers). Close by framing the rest of the unit around how teachers structure that deliberate practice.

title: The Pre-Listening Stage: Building the Bridge
brief: Explain the purpose of pre-listening work using the detailed lesson-plan example from the source: the teacher displays pictures related to the topic, asks students to identify what is happening, activates prior vocabulary, and builds schemata about the situation students will hear. Draw directly on the source's stated rationale for each step — creating interest, activating prior knowledge, involving students, and addressing select vocabulary items from the listening text in a contextualised manner so that vocabulary presentation appeals to oral/aural and visual learners. Emphasise the source's point that this stage sets expectations and situations about what students will hear, and show how pre-teaching key items (the source gives 'take a statement', 'accident report', 'come out of nowhere') reduces the chance of learners panicking when the audio begins.

title: Listening for Gist: The First-Listen Task
brief: Use the source's lesson-plan example to show how a first listening is designed for gist only. The source explicitly names 'listening for gist and detail' as the skills focus and shows the teacher telling students: 'You are going to hear about a situation… The first time you listen you do not need your textbook.' Explain what this instruction achieves — removing the written text reduces cognitive overload and keeps attention on meaning. Draw on the source's broader point that teachers can play a short audio text and ask students to take notes, then discuss in small groups, to illustrate how a gist task can feed directly into peer interaction. Keep the focus on first-listen design; detail tasks are covered in the next section.

title: Listening for Detail: Returning to the Audio
brief: Show how the same audio is used again for a more focused purpose, drawing on the source's lesson objectives, which distinguish between determining main ideas and identifying specific details in the same listening text. Use the source's note that students 'will get to hear the dialogue more than once' as the practical principle: repeated listening with a changed task is the mechanism. Connect this to the source's game-based summary activity — groups write the most detailed and accurate summary they can, the class votes or the teacher decides — as a concrete post-detail-listening task sequence. Also draw on the source's 'focused listening' skill label, which appears across multiple lesson descriptions in the art-activities source, to show that this kind of targeted, purposeful listening is a recurring classroom goal.

title: The Post-Listening Stage: Using What Was Heard
brief: Explain that post-listening work extends the audio into productive language use, drawing on the source's lesson plan where students move from listening into an information-gap speaking activity using the same vocabulary and grammar encountered in the text. The source states that the situations from the listening will be used in the info-gap activity later in the lesson (schemata building/scaffolding), making the connection between stages explicit. Also draw on the source's suggestion that teachers incorporate open-ended questions at the end of class requiring students to reflect on what they learned and how they could apply it, as a model for reflective post-listening closure. Stress that the post-listening stage should feel like a natural continuation, not a separate lesson.

title: Practical Task Sequences: Putting the Stages Together
brief: Bring the three stages together into a reusable classroom sequence, drawing on the complete lesson-plan example in the source as the model. Walk through the full arc: warm-up pictures activate prior knowledge → vocabulary pre-teaching reduces panic → gist listen without textbook → detail listen with focused questions → post-listening speaking or writing task. Use the source's 'focused listening' skill label — which appears in lesson descriptions across beginner-to-advanced levels in the art-activities source — to show that this staged approach is applicable at multiple proficiency levels, not only intermediate. Close with the source's caution about time management: extending one activity and ignoring others can prevent the class from achieving lesson goals, reminding teachers to plan each stage with a realistic time allocation.
